reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: A functional anorectal pain disorder marked by a chronic or recurrent dull ache or pressure high in the rectum, often worse with sitting
Episodes typically last twenty minutes or longer, distinguishing it from the brief attacks of proctalgia fugax
Digital rectal examination classically reproduces the pain on posterior traction of the puborectalis, which is often tender and tight
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, so structural, inflammatory, and neoplastic causes of anorectal pain must first be ruled out
Associated with pelvic floor tension, psychological stress, and dyssynergic defecation
Management is conservative and directed at the pelvic floor: reassurance, warm baths, pelvic floor physiotherapy and biofeedback, digital massage, and muscle-relaxation or neuromodulation strategies
Overlaps with other functional pelvic floor and defecatory disorders
reference.pathophysiology: Levator ani syndrome is thought to arise from chronic spasm and tension of the pelvic floor muscles, particularly the puborectalis and levator ani, producing a persistent aching or pressure sensation high in the rectum. There is no structural lesion; central and peripheral pain sensitisation, pelvic floor dyssynergia, and psychological stress are all implicated. It sits within the spectrum of functional anorectal pain, sharing mechanisms with proctalgia fugax and dyssynergic defecation.
additionalDifferentials: Endometriosis or other gynaecological pelvic pain
additionalInvestigations: Digital rectal examination assessing puborectalis tenderness and pain on traction
Proctoscopy or sigmoidoscopy to exclude mucosal disease
Anorectal manometry and balloon expulsion to assess for dyssynergia
Defecography where obstructed defecation is suspected
Pelvic MRI or cross-sectional imaging to exclude structural or neoplastic causes
Colonoscopy where alarm features or age warrant exclusion of malignancy
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a palpable mass suggesting malignancy
Nocturnal or progressive pain unresponsive to conservative measures
Neurological deficit suggesting a sacral or cauda equina lesion
New anorectal pain in an older patient without a prior functional history
reference.prognosis: A benign but often chronic and relapsing condition; many patients improve with pelvic floor physiotherapy, biofeedback, and reassurance, though symptoms can persist or recur.
pitfalls: Labelling anorectal pain as functional without excluding structural or neoplastic disease
Overlooking coexisting dyssynergic defecation amenable to biofeedback
Repeated ineffective surgery for presumed fissure or haemorrhoids
Underestimating the contribution of psychological stress and pelvic floor tension
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
management: Reassurance and explanation of the benign functional nature of the disorder
Pelvic-floor physiotherapy and biofeedback to retrain and relax the puborectalis
Digital transrectal massage of the levator ani and warm sitz baths for symptomatic relief
Electrogalvanic stimulation and neuromodulation strategies for refractory pain
Address dyssynergic defecation and treat coexisting constipation
Diagnosis of exclusion: rule out structural, inflammatory and neoplastic anorectal disease first
Psychological support for associated stress and chronic pain
